cues.text: A Martyr of Bare Historical Fact
As the Catholic Encyclopedia frankly acknowledges after careful modern investigation, remarkably little can be said with certainty about George beyond the essential fact of his martyrdom.
He suffered at or near Lydda (also called Diospolis) in Palestine, probably before the reign of Constantine.
He was venerated from a very early date as one of the greatest martyrs of the Eastern Church, where he is known simply as 'the Great Martyr.'
A Soldier Under Diocletian

Later tradition, considerably embellished over the centuries, holds that George was a Roman soldier, possibly of Cappadocian Greek descent, who rose to a position of some standing in the Praetorian Guard under Emperor Diocletian.

When Diocletian launched his empire-wide persecution of Christians in 303, George, a secret believer, refused to comply with the order to sacrifice to the Roman gods, was denounced, tortured at length, and finally beheaded — traditionally dated to April 23.
The Legend of the Dragon
The famous story of George slaying a dragon to save a princess and an entire city is the tale for which he is best remembered in popular imagination.

As the Catholic Encyclopedia notes, it is 'a very late development' that cannot be traced earlier than the twelfth or thirteenth century, appearing in its familiar form in Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend .

Whatever its symbolic origins, the legend is a medieval addition rather than an ancient historical memory, and some scholars have proposed connections with older pagan or classical dragon-slaying traditions, while the precise origins of the legend remain disputed.
Ancient and Widespread Veneration
Despite the scarcity of reliable biographical detail, Devotion to George spread with extraordinary speed and reach from a very early date.
A late-fifth-century text traditionally associated with Pope Gelasius I lists George among martyrs whose 'names are justly reverenced among men, but whose actions are known only to God'.
This was evidence that even by the late fifth century, legendary elaborations had already begun to obscure a genuinely ancient historical martyrdom.
Patron of Warriors and Nations

Devotion to George received an enormous boost during the Crusades, when later accounts associated Christian victories with the saint and King Richard the Lionheart was said to have placed his campaigns under George's protection.
England's devotion was cemented when King Edward III named him the kingdom's patron in the fourteenth century and founded the Order of the Garter under his protection.
This has made George one of the most widely claimed patron saints in the Christian world, also honored by Georgia, Ethiopia, Catalonia, Aragon, Ukraine, and the city of Moscow.
Legacy
George remains one of the Fourteen Holy Helpers and among the most universally recognized of all Christian martyr-saints.

His image as the dragon-slaying knight in shining armor — however late a medieval invention — has become a permanent and beloved symbol across cultures for courage in the face of evil and the ultimate victory of good.
